To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
self-ratings of affect are very highly correlated with similarity judgments and that the two data types can be used interchangeably to derive structural models of affect.
self-ratings and similarity judgments of the same affective states contain very high correlations, and that this finding has far-reaching implications for affect structure research.

(1) the similarity judgments of affect, when used as a starting point for structural analyses, are essentially equivalent to correlations of affect ratings; (2) the high correspondence between similarity judgments of affect and correlations of affect ratings is found both at the global structural level and in local subgroups of affect; (3) the high correspondence is not an artifact of the particular similarity judgment method used; and (4) the high correspondence cannot be explained by the use of a common metric for both data types.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether similarity judgments of affect can be used to study the structure of affect.
the question of whether the structural information in similarity judgments is the same as the structural information in correlations computed from self-rating data.
the question of whether the structural information contained in similarity judgments and self-rating correlations of affects is the same.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
self-report measures are valid, but not very reliable.
the data from similarity judgments and self-ratings are essentially identical in their structure.

both self-rating correlations and affect similarity judgments are equally valid starting-points for the structural analysis of affect, and both data types are capable to reveal the same basic structural information.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the structure of affective space is best understood in terms of the covariations of affects in experience.
self-rating correlations are a valid starting point for affect structure research.

self-rating correlations of affects and similarity judgments of them are equally valid starting-points for structural analyses of affects, and that the models that have been derived by using them are equally valid.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the two data types should be considered as equally valid sources of information for the structural analysis of affect.

affect structure research can benefit from a more systematic use of similarity judgments, which are less susceptible to response biases than self-rating data and can be collected in a fraction of the time.
the use of similarity judgment data in affect structure research should be considered a viable and potentially useful alternative to the use of self-rating correlations.
